conflicts.note: Even with documented Rolex-to-Royal-Family provenance on one example examined by Ku, the source concludes the truth is unsettled and the 'obsidian' name is likely collector terminology rather than a Rolex designation.
positions: Hairspring (the article's author) and Eric Ku argue the most likely answer is that these are dyed onyx dials that have de-bonded/discoloured over time — they don't look like obsidian to a gemologist, the 'lifting' ring around the handstack recurs too consistently to be natural veining, and a known-onyx Patek dial of similar appearance supports the onyx-degradation theory.
An alternative reading is that they are genuinely obsidian dials where the protective varnish has reacted with the adhesive; a third (least likely per the author) is that they are simply fake.

conflicts.note: The catalogue evidence makes a strong case for factory lavender, at least as a Japan-market option, but the topic remains debated in the wider collector community.
positions: Hodinkee-style 'tropical / changed-over-time' interpretation: these started life as grey or silver and shifted hue.

Wind Vintage / Eric Wind position, supported by a 1972 Rolex Japan catalogue scan, that lavender was a factory dial option — bolstered by no-lume examples whose paint shouldn't have been affected by tritium and which present a consistent, edge-to-edge lavender hue.
conflicts.topic: Whether lavender 1601 dials are factory-original or aged grey/silver dials

conflicts.note: Mentioned here because Oysterquartz Datejusts share this lineage; treat the Genta attribution as contested.
positions: James Dowling attributes the predecessor ref. 5100 'Texan' (and by extension the Oysterquartz aesthetic) to Gérald Genta.
Brandon Baines's Fratello article on Rolex's 'Nautilina' disputes the Genta attribution.
conflicts.topic: Authorship of the Oysterquartz design lineage

consensus.claim: The Datejust was introduced in 1945 to mark Rolex's 40th anniversary; the first reference was the 4467, only in precious metals, on the newly created Jubilee bracelet.

The name 'Datejust' was not printed on the dial until 1953; Rolex had also considered the names 'Victory' (deemed too politically charged after WWII), 'Ritedate' (registered in October 1945), and 'Jubilee'.
The Datejust was Rolex's flagship before the Day-Date arrived in 1956; the precious-metal-only-plus-signature-bracelet template pioneered by the Datejust was then carried over to the Day-Date.
The fluted bezel debuted around 1953 on the steel ref. 6305, replacing the earlier finely-toothed 'reeded' bezel that had been broadly used across the industry.
The Cyclops magnifying lens was added to the Datejust in the mid-1950s (the 63xx generation) and has remained a Rolex signature.

The 16xx generation (ref. 1600 smooth, 1601 fluted, 1602 engine-turned, 1603 engine-turned steel, plus gold variants like 1601/8) ran from 1959 to 1977 and is when the Datejust took the shape it broadly retains today.
The 1601 fluted bezel is always executed in precious metal (typically white gold on steel-cased examples); the 1603's engine-turned bezel was almost always steel, though gold versions exist.
The 16xx generation is characterised by the stepped 'pie-pan' dial, where the outer minute track is sloped downward, giving the dial visible depth.

16xx watches use Aegler-produced caliber 1565 (18,000vph) from launch, replaced by caliber 1575 (19,800vph) in 1965; a hacking seconds function was added in 1972 without changing the caliber number. Neither offers a quickset date.
Movements in this family are often plate-stamped '1560' or '1570' (the no-date versions of the calibers); Rolex used the same number-engraved bridges across the family.

The 16xxx five-digit generation was introduced in 1977 (16014 fluted steel, 16000 smooth, 16013 two-tone, 16030 engine-turned, 16018 yellow gold, 16019 white gold). It introduced the new quickset caliber 3035 (28,800vph, ~50h reserve) and replaced the pie-pan with a flat dial; gold versions also gained sapphire crystals while steel/two-tone kept acrylic.

The 1988 162xx generation brought sapphire crystals across the line and the upgraded caliber 3135 (full balance bridge, larger balance wheel, 31 jewels), which then powered Datejust three-handers for roughly three decades until being replaced in 2019.
The full-size vintage Datejust is 36mm with 20mm lugs, a screw-down crown, screw-in caseback, and a water resistance rating that on modern examples is 100m.

The Jubilee bracelet was created for the original 1945 Datejust and remains the model-signature bracelet, though Oyster was also offered and dealers historically swapped bracelets to suit customers, so original pairings vary.

Vintage Jubilee bracelets exist in folded (older) and solid-link (from roughly 1974) versions; American- and Mexican-produced Jubilees have oval rather than flat-bottomed links, and clasp configurations (e.g. crown overhanging the clasp) indicate market of original sale.

Vintage Datejust dials were supplied by Singer, Beyeler, Lemmerig and Stern, and dial-printing cliches were originally hand-cut, so there is genuine and significant variation in fonts, serifs, and stroke thickness on otherwise correct factory dials.

The standard dial text reads 'Superlative Chronometer Officially Certified'; rare earlier 'OCC' dials reading only 'Officially Certified Chronometer' exist, as do a few 1970 prototype dials with floating 'Swiss' under the SCOC line.

Applied indices come in a wide vocabulary of shapes — simple sticks, 'Bon-Bon-Blocs' in one or two widths, 'barn', bell-shaped, black-topped, rectangular 'pool' (lume-filled), 'doorstop', and faceted variants among them.

No-lume dials (often called 'Japan dials') were produced for markets with import restrictions on radioactive materials such as Japan; Rolex used the regular printed dials, so a 'T Swiss T' designation can appear even where there is no tritium, and the matching handset is closed/no-lume.

Beyond the standard fluted, smooth and engine-turned bezels, earlier and rarer variants include Morellis, Bamboo, Zephyr, Moreau, Moiré and the 'Florentine' bezel (e.g. on ref. 6520 with matching brick bracelet).

Exotic dial families that appear in the vintage Datejust include linen (subtle crosshatch), tapestry (vertical-pattern), Buckley (painted Roman numerals), 'Wide Boy' (oversized markers), wood (e.g. burl, birch), and stone dials (onyx, malachite, tiger eye, lapis, etc., generally fitted only to gold cases).

Rolex stone dials are not solid slabs of stone — they are a thin layer of stone bonded to a metal base plate that then fits the movement; this construction affects how the dial ages and can craze or delaminate over time.

Lavender no-lume dials were a factory option for the 1601: a 1972 Rolex Japan catalogue documents lavender as one of the available dial colours (alongside more familiar tones), supporting the case that surviving examples are original rather than discoloured grey dials.
Vintage 36mm Oyster cases like the Datejust's are renowned for daily wearability — slim, light, sturdy, with the same case architecture also used by the contemporaneous Explorer.
The first run of 100 Datejusts, presented in 1945 at the Hôtel des Bergues in Geneva, carried unique numbering rather than the regular serial or reference engravings.

In 1956 Rolex introduced caliber 1065, a slimmer automatic that did away with the protruding 'bubbleback' case shape; alpha and dagger handsets gave way to the pencil/baton hands now associated with the Datejust by the late 1950s.

marks.explanation: Stepped 16xx-generation dial where the outer minute-track ring is sloped downward off a raised centre, giving the dial visible depth. Disappeared with the flat dials of the 16xxx generation in 1977.
marks.name: Pie-pan dial

marks.explanation: 2.5× magnifier fused to the crystal over the date aperture; introduced on Datejust in the mid-1950s and now a Rolex signature.
marks.name: Cyclops

marks.explanation: Independently advanced date wheel via the crown. Arrived with caliber 3035 in the 1977 16xxx generation; the earlier 16xx generation (incl. 1601) lacks it and requires advancing the hands through 24h to change the date.
marks.name: Quickset date

marks.explanation: Dial executed without radium/tritium plots and paired with closed, lume-less hands for markets that restricted radioactive imports (notably Japan). The base printed dials were the same, so the 'T Swiss T' marking can still appear even when no tritium is present.
marks.name: Japan dial / no-lume dial

marks.explanation: Painted Roman numeral dial variant found on five-digit Datejusts (e.g. 16030); collector nickname rather than a Rolex designation.
marks.name: Buckley dial

marks.explanation: Subtle fine crosshatch pattern mimicking textile weave; most often found in the 16xx and 16xxx Datejust generations and also used on Day-Dates.
marks.name: Linen dial

marks.explanation: Vertical-pattern textured dial variant found in both five-digit and sapphire-era Datejusts (e.g. 16014, 16234).
marks.name: Tapestry dial

marks.explanation: Dial variant with oversized baton markers and hands found on some 16xx references; a collector nickname.
marks.name: Wide Boy

marks.explanation: Rare early dial reading 'Officially Certified Chronometer' rather than the later 'Superlative Chronometer Officially Certified'; usually associated with gilt-era references like the 6305.
marks.name: OCC dial

marks.explanation: Collector vocabulary for the various applied-index shapes found across vintage Datejust dials; useful for spotting period-correct vs. service or fake dials.
marks.name: Bon-Bon-Blocs / doorstop / barn / bell / pool indices

marks.explanation: Early Jubilees used hollow, folded links; Rolex transitioned to half-solid (solid outer links) around 1974 within the 16xx era — so this is not a clean handover at the 16xxx changeover as is sometimes claimed.
marks.name: Folded vs. solid Jubilee

marks.explanation: Domed bezel with very fine teeth used on early Datejusts (pre-fluted); broadly used across the industry at the time and replaced on Datejust by the fluted bezel around 1953.
marks.name: Reeded bezel

marks.explanation: Vintage white-gold Datejusts (e.g. 16019) show a small infill on the inside corners of the lugs, mirroring Day-Date midcase construction — a useful field-ID detail since they otherwise look like steel.
marks.name: White-gold-lug tell

model_context: The Datejust is Rolex's archetypal date-on-dial watch, introduced in 1945 as the brand's 40th-anniversary flagship and the first wristwatch with an automatically and instantly changing date. Originally produced only in precious metals on the then-new Jubilee bracelet, it eventually expanded to steel (1953, ref. 6305) and two-tone. The 16xx generation (1959–1977) is where the watch settled into its now-iconic form: Cyclops crystal, fluted/smooth/engine-turned bezel options, pie-pan dial, baton hands. References 1601 (fluted white-gold bezel) and 16014 (its five-digit successor with quickset date, sapphire came later with 162xx) anchor this page. The Datejust's appeal is its near-universal wearability, mechanical robustness, and a near-endless variety of dials, bezels, bracelets and materials — which is also the source of the demand: a buyer can specify a Datejust into almost any role from formal to casual.

module_candidates.rationale: Distinct case architecture, caliber 5035, 25-year production run (1977–2002), contested Genta lineage and a growing pre-owned following — deserves its own page rather than crowding the 1601/16014 reference.
A spin-off line with a rotating bezel (e.g. 1625, 116263, 116264) that is functionally and visually distinct from the standard Datejust and routinely treated as 'adopted family' rather than core.
The 41mm sizing experiment is a separate era with its own movements (3136, later 3235) and a different design intent; warrants its own write-up so the vintage 1601/16014 page can stay focused.

Pie-pan vs flat, linen, tapestry, Buckley, Wide Boy, wood (burl/birch), stone (onyx/malachite/tiger eye/lapis), no-lume/Japan, lavender — a standalone illustrated taxonomy would serve buyers far better than scattered references.

module_candidates.module: Spotting a fake or refinished vintage Datejust dial
module_candidates.rationale: Already a self-contained tutorial in the corpus (blank stamping, font, coronet, applique geometry, lume behaviour); pairs naturally with the dial taxonomy as buyer-protection content.
6305 is the inflection point — first steel Datejust, introduction of the fluted bezel, and the run-up to the Cyclops — a focused page on this reference would anchor the pre-16xx story.
Pre-1959 references with bubbleback cases, dauphine/leaf hands, coin-edge bezels and gilt OCC dials are mechanically and aesthetically a different watch from the 1601, and currently underserved here.

Tiger eye, malachite, lapis, and the 'obsidian/onyx' debate together form a rich subject that would benefit from its own piece — including the construction note (stone bonded to a metal base plate) and the Eric Ku / Loupe This investigation.

source_contributions.unique_contribution: Author's deep dive into the 1601 specifically: 1959 introduction, caliber 1565→1575 transition in 1965, hacking added 1972, and the observation that movements are often '1560/1570' plate-stamped. Also documents the 'Japan dial' no-lume execution with closed handset.

Names Rolex considered ('Ritedate' registered Oct 1, 1945; 'Jubilee'; 'Victory'); the first batch of 100 watches at Hôtel des Bergues with unique numbering; introduction of caliber 1065 in 1956 ending the bubbleback case; transition from alpha/dagger to pencil hands in the late 1950s.

Catalogue of dial suppliers (Singer, Beyeler, Lemmerig, Stern); the 'OCC' dial variant and 1970 floating-'Swiss' prototype; the full taxonomy of index shapes ('Bon-Bon-Blocs', barn, bell, doorstop, faceted, pool); rare bezel variants Morellis/Bamboo/Zephyr/Moreau/Moiré; the American vs. Mexican Jubilee link-profile distinction.

Buying-guide framing: the four-digit/five-digit/sapphire-generation taxonomy as the practical decision tree for a vintage Datejust buyer; note that the half-solid Jubilee with solid outer links was actually phased in around 1974 within the 16xx era, not at the 16xxx changeover (a common misconception).

Hands-on authentication checklist: blank stamping (pie-pan step sharpness, date-aperture and centre-hole geometry), coronet shape and prong definition, applied-index finishing, lume aging (tritium should now be visually dead; modern LumiNova lighting up is a tell of replacement or relume) — plus the caveat that real dials also have imperfect printing.

Reproduces evidence (via Wind Vintage/Charlie Dunne) of a 1972 Rolex Japan catalogue page showing lavender as a factory dial colour, supporting the view that lavender 1601 dials are factory-original rather than discoloured.
Notes that no-lume dials should not age the way tritium dials do (no lume to bleed/affect the paint), which is one reason surviving lavender examples appear so clean.

Detailed construction note that Rolex stone dials are stone bonded to a metal base (not solid slabs), and the ongoing debate around 'obsidian' 1600 dials — including the Eric Ku / Loupe This Oman provenance investigation that suggests these are dyed onyx dials that have delaminated/discoloured rather than true obsidian.

Close documentation of an unusually well-preserved blue-dial 1600 with smooth bezel and folded 6251 Jubilee, including discussion of typical condition pitfalls on 16xx (dial deterioration around the handstack, lume pips, date window edge, and dial edge).

Documentation of the 16030 metallic black dial variant and the dial 'family' on five-digit references (glossy, matte, confetti / red-and-green-fleck, metallic) plus practical buying notes on lume-plot loss and incorrect-era dials.
Documents the very plain blue-stick-dial smooth-bezel 16200 on a matte 78360 Oyster — drilled lugs, stamped end-links, tritium — as an unusually pared-back configuration in the line.

Personal-history portrait of a long-worn 16220 (engine-turned bezel, blue dial, 3135) given as an 80th-birthday gift in 1996 and showing real-world unpolished-case patina, including a dental-floss-under-the-bracelet anecdote that explains corresponding crystal fogging.

Documents a white-gold 16019 with burl-wood radial dial on a riveted Oyster bracelet, and the visual tell of white-gold Datejust cases — small infill on the inside corners of the lugs (also noted in the Hodinkee Bring a Loupe column).
Spotting tip for white-gold vintage Datejusts: look for the small infill on the inside corners of the lugs, mimicking the Day-Date midcase construction; useful field-ID detail.
Full-gold Datejust survey: ref. 6105 (1950–1953, caliber A296, 18,000vph, alpha hands, arrow indices) and the structural shift at 16018 (sapphire on gold while steel/two-tone kept acrylic).
Walkthrough of the stone-dial (tiger-eye, malachite) and textile-pattern (linen, tapestry) dial families and which references they are typically found in.
Documents the 41mm Datejust II (introduced 2009, replaced by the Datejust 41 in 2016) as a short-lived sizing experiment, including its caliber 3136 and Chromalight lume usage.

Background on the Oysterquartz Datejust: caliber 5035 (chronometer-certified, 11 jewels, 32 kHz, five years of development), production 1977–2002, and the disputed Gérald Genta attribution for its predecessor ref. 5100 'Texan'.

stories.title: Patrick Bateman's 'Don't touch the watch' — the Datejust in American Psycho
stories.why: One of the model's signature pop-culture moments and a reminder that the Datejust's recognisability extends well beyond watch enthusiasts.

stories.title: The 1996 80th-birthday 16220
stories.why: A blue-dial engine-turned 16220 given to a dentist on his 80th birthday and worn daily for 17 years — including the watchmaker discovering green-wax dental-floss residue under the crown that had eaten into the dial paint above the date window. A vivid illustration of how Datejusts are actually lived with.

stories.title: Gigi Buffon's one-hand skeletonised Datejust by Artisans de Genève
stories.why: Italian goalkeeper Gianluigi Buffon commissioned Artisans de Genève to rebuild a Datejust as a single-handed, skeletonised watch with a bi-material dial, a Clous-de-Paris bezel referencing a goal net, and a flame-blued hand with a hand-painted red tip — a notable example of post-factory Datejust personalisation (independent, not authorised by Rolex).

stories.title: The first hundred 1945 Datejusts at the Hôtel des Bergues
stories.why: The model's launch event in Geneva used a batch of 100 watches carrying unique numbering instead of regular serials and reference engravings — an early 'special edition' before special editions were a thing.

stories.title: The 1972 Rolex Japan catalogue and the lavender dial
stories.why: A catalogue scan surfaced by Charlie Dunne at Wind Vintage that documents lavender as a factory dial colour — meaningful evidence in a long-running debate about whether lavender 1601 dials are original.
